clue.text: Safe to put on an overcoat?

parts.note: peter is old criminal slang for a safe, as in a peterman or safecracker
to put on an act is to sham, to pretend

explanation.surface: A question about whether a strongbox could be worn over a coat.
explanation.walkthrough: PETER is underworld slang for a safe; 'to put on' (feign) gives SHAM. The question mark flags the odd picture of wearing a safe.
explanation.definitionFit: A petersham is a heavy woollen greatcoat named after Viscount Petersham, so it is a kind of outer garment.

clue.text: Browning's girl I spotted in Threepenny Opera, finally

indicators.note: something spotted in a place is seen within it, so this letter sits inside the next piece

parts.note: three pennies, each abbreviated P, give three Ps

indicators.note: finally asks for the closing letter of the word Opera

explanation.surface: A Browning heroine claims to have seen herself in Brecht's Threepenny Opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Threepenny' is split into three P (penny) letters; 'spotted in' puts I among them to make PIPP, and 'finally' takes the A ending Opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Pippa is the silk-winding heroine of Robert Browning's verse drama Pippa Passes.

clue.text: Spot trains, changing on the hour

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece is placed on another, so these letters follow on below
the letters of trains are changing their order, a rearrangement signal

parts.note: h is the standard abbreviation for hour

explanation.surface: A trainspotter watches trains switching platforms exactly on the hour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spot' looks like trainspotting but is a verb meaning to stain; 'changing' is the anagram signal and 'on' places H (hour) last in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To tarnish is to stain or sully, which is what spotting a reputation or surface does.

clue.text: R Crusoe, wrecked, found quarters and supplies

indicators.note: a wrecked thing is broken up, so these letters are knocked into a new order

parts.note: east and south are compass quarters, abbreviated E and S

explanation.surface: Robinson Crusoe, shipwrecked, finds lodging and provisions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrecked' shuffles R CRUSOE together with E and S (two compass quarters) into the nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Resources are stocks or reserves of material to draw on, the same thing as stores or provisions.

clue.text: Is one called out to the shires?

definitions.text: Is one called out to the shires?

parts.words: Is one called out to the shires?
parts.note: read as a country visit it seems a rural question, but shires are the heavy shire horses and the person summoned treats them

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a professional gets summoned to the rural counties.
explanation.walkthrough: Shire horses are big draught horses; a vet called out to them is the hyphenated answer. The shires are also England's rural counties, the false trail.
explanation.definitionFit: A vet who treats horses, an equine veterinary surgeon, is informally given this name.

clue.text: How many of the Irish nominally start in Ulster?

definitions.text: How many of the Irish nominally start in Ulster?

parts.words: How many of the Irish nominally start in Ulster?
parts.note: seems to ask a census question, but nominally means by name: many Irish surnames begin with the same prefix

explanation.surface: Someone asks how many Irish people make their start in Ulster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'How many' does not want a number: many Irish and Scottish surnames begin with the Gaelic prefix meaning 'son of'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mac is the Gaelic surname prefix meaning son of, opening names like MacMahon and MacNeill.

clue.text: Young Bobby, not the eldest son

definitions.meaning: a bobby is a British policeman, so a young one is a police trainee
in family terms this word means a younger son or the junior branch of a family

explanation.surface: A young boy named Bobby who is not his parents' firstborn.
explanation.walkthrough: Bobby is British slang for a police officer, not a boy's name here.
explanation.definitionFit: A police trainee bears this title, and traditionally so does a younger son not in line to inherit.

clue.text: One carrying pelt of American mammal

indicators.note: one carrying something has it on its back, so the two pieces are joined together

parts.note: an animal's pelt is its fur coat
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: Someone carries the skin of an animal from the Americas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carrying' simply joins COAT (pelt) and I (one).
explanation.definitionFit: The coati is a long-snouted raccoon relative of Central and South America.

clue.text: Abandon hope for literary giant

definitions.meaning: to give up all expectation, a verb sense
a giant of literature here means an actual giant in a book

explanation.surface: Someone gives up hope of becoming a great writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'literary giant' looks like a great author, but it is Giant Despair, who imprisons Christian in Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose all expectation of success is the verb sense; Bunyan's allegory names its castle ogre after hopelessness.

clue.text: Waterproof material hearty tent-maker has at home

parts.note: hearties is an old name for sailors, and a tar is a sailor
St Paul worked as a tentmaker, according to Acts
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: A jolly tentmaker keeps rainproof fabric at his house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hearty' is a noun here, a sailor (TAR); the tent-maker is St Paul.
explanation.definitionFit: A tarpaulin is heavy canvas or plastic sheeting made rainproof, used as a cover.

clue.text: One who checks documents for every employer

parts.note: per means for each, as in miles per hour
one who employs a tool or method uses it, so is its user

explanation.surface: A clerk verifies paperwork for each company that hires.
explanation.walkthrough: 'employer' is not a boss: it is one who employs, that is uses, something.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who reads through papers carefully is examining them, so is a reader of documents.

clue.text: Less well bred dog or horse, say

indicators.note: say signals that the word is spoken, so we want something pronounced like it

parts.note: a courser is a swift horse, and also a hound used in coursing hares

explanation.surface: Comparing which animal, a dog or a horse, has poorer breeding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' asks for a word heard the same as COURSER, a word for a hound or a swift horse.
explanation.definitionFit: Coarser means cruder or more vulgar in manner, the opposite of refined.

clue.text: A decline accepted by society for so long

indicators.note: the preceding letters are taken on by the next piece, so they are joined to it

parts.note: to die away is to decline and fade
U stands for upper-class or polite society, as in U and non-U

explanation.surface: An accepted social downturn lasting a long time.
explanation.walkthrough: U is the old label for upper-class usage and polite society, as in 'U and non-U'. 'so long' is a farewell, not a length of time.
explanation.definitionFit: Both expressions are goodbyes, said when parting from someone.

clue.text: Mexican food left in derelict hacienda

indicators.note: the left letter goes in among the shuffled letters
something derelict is ruined, so these letters fall into a new order

explanation.surface: Some Mexican dish was abandoned in a ruined ranch house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'derelict' rearranges HACIENDA and 'in' puts L (left) inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An enchilada is a rolled tortilla with a filling, baked in chilli sauce, a staple dish of Mexico.

clue.text: Peaceful life together possible in exotic scene

indicators.note: a possible version of these words is one of their other arrangements, an anagram signal

explanation.surface: Living in harmony might be achievable in some faraway setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exotic' looks like the anagram signal, but it is fodder: 'possible' rearranges EXOTIC SCENE.
explanation.definitionFit: Coexistence is living alongside others without conflict, as in the Cold War phrase peaceful coexistence.

clue.text: Like Henry Wood?

parts.note: as means like, in the manner of
H is the symbol for the henry, the SI unit of inductance

explanation.surface: A question about resembling Sir Henry Wood, the conductor who founded the Proms.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Wood was a famous English conductor; here 'Henry' is H, the unit of inductance, and 'Wood' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Ash is a hardwood tree and its timber, used for tool handles and bats.

clue.text: A new suggestion with reference to extra fare

parts.note: a tip is a hint or piece of advice
as to means concerning, with regard to

explanation.surface: A fresh proposal concerning an additional fee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fare' is food here, not a ticket price: an extra course before the main meal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian starter course of cold meats and pickles is food served besides the main dish.

clue.text: Boy in school head's expelled as danger to heahh?

indicators.note: the clue word that signals this step
the head of a school is its first letter, and expelling it removes that letter

parts.note: Lester is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A pupil is expelled because the headteacher thinks he threatens wellbeing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heahh' is a misprint for 'health' on the page. School loses its head (S), giving CHOOL, and the boy LESTER goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: High blood levels of this fatty substance clog arteries, so it is a hazard to wellbeing.

clue.text: Circus act stoned on hemp product?

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece is placed on top of the second

parts.note: stoned is slang for intoxicated, as is tight
rope is traditionally twisted from hemp fibre

explanation.surface: A performer is high while working with a cannabis product.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stoned' and 'hemp' suggest drugs, but TIGHT means drunk and hemp makes ROPE.
explanation.definitionFit: Walking a taut high wire is a classic big-top performance.

clue.text: Order scenery, working as chapel member?

parts.note: an order is a class or sort, a type
the setting of a play is its scenery

explanation.surface: A stage manager ordering scenery is like a member of a church congregation.
explanation.walkthrough: A chapel is the name for a union branch in a printing works, so a chapel member is a printer setting type.
explanation.definitionFit: Composing pages from metal letters was the work of print compositors, whose union branches were chapels.

clue.text: Softwood pipe mender

parts.note: soft in music is piano, abbreviated P
lumber is sawn timber, the American word for wood

explanation.surface: A tradesman uses pine to repair a pipe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Softwood' looks like pine timber; split it as 'soft' (P, piano) plus 'wood' (LUMBER).
explanation.definitionFit: A tradesman who fits and repairs water pipes and drains.

clue.text: Vehicle that goes out when service has been successfully dealt with

definitions.meaning: a covered road vehicle for goods

definitions.text: that goes out when service has been successfully dealt with
definitions.meaning: in tennis scoring, ... is short for advantage, and ... out is called when the receiver wins the point after deuce

explanation.surface: A truck leaves once a repair service is finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'service' is a tennis serve: when the receiver returns it well after deuce the score is 'van out', receiver's advantage.
explanation.definitionFit: A box-shaped goods vehicle, and also tennis shorthand for advantage, as in the scoring call van out.

clue.text: Judgment of court in support of composer

indicators.note: in a down clue a piece in support of another sits beneath it

parts.note: Giuseppe Verdi was the Italian operatic composer

explanation.surface: A ruling by a court that backs a composer's claim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in support of' places CT (court) under VERDI in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A verdict is the decision a jury or judge reaches on a case.

clue.text: Dives in which dog caught vermin

parts.note: Pluto is Mickey Mouse's dog in Disney cartoons
c is the cricket scoring abbreviation for caught
a rat is a typical pest

explanation.surface: A dog catches pests in some seedy bars.
explanation.walkthrough: Dives is the rich man in the Bible parable of Dives and Lazarus, not shady bars.
explanation.definitionFit: The rich man of the Lazarus parable is the archetypal wealthy person, someone ruling by riches.

clue.text: Deliveries of removal firms, not using motorway

indicators.note: not using a thing means leaving it out, so that letter goes

parts.note: removal firms move house contents, so they are movers
M is the abbreviation for motorway, as in the M1

explanation.surface: Removal companies make deliveries without taking the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled; 'Deliveries' means these, not parcels.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricket over is a set of six balls bowled, so overs are batches of bowled balls.

clue.text: Trunk carried by actors overseas

indicators.note: the answer is carried inside the letters of the next words

explanation.surface: A travelling company of actors takes a large chest abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carried by' takes the letters running across 'acTORS Overseas'.
explanation.definitionFit: The torso is the body's trunk, without head or limbs.

clue.text: Work hard on one run — whence a precious cargo?

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils
I is the Roman numeral one
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: Toiling on one voyage, a ship asks where its valuable freight came from.
explanation.walkthrough: Ophir is the biblical land of gold to which Solomon's ships sailed, and the starting point in Masefield's poem Cargoes.
explanation.definitionFit: Solomon's fleets brought gold from this biblical land, the source of a valuable shipment.

clue.text: National issue

definitions.meaning: a national, as a noun, is a citizen of a state
an issue under discussion is a matter or topic

explanation.surface: A matter of nationwide concern.
explanation.definitionFit: A citizen owing allegiance to a crown is one, and a topic under discussion is another sense.

clue.text: Bill cricketer picked up

indicators.note: in a down clue picking up raises the word so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: a bat is a batsman in cricket

explanation.surface: A cricketer's restaurant tab is collected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'picked up' turns BAT upwards in the down entry; a bat is a batsman.
explanation.definitionFit: A tab is a running account at a bar, an invoice to be settled.

clue.text: Archaeological find sets hot line buzzing

indicators.note: buzzing suggests agitated movement, so these letters are shaken up

explanation.surface: An archaeological discovery makes the hotline ring constantly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'buzzing' rearranges HOT LINE.
explanation.definitionFit: A neolith is a polished stone tool from the New Stone Age, an artefact dug up on sites.

clue.text: Plant producing car once with no starter

indicators.note: the starter of a word is its first letter, which is dropped

parts.note: Morris was an old British car make, as in the Morris Minor

explanation.surface: A plant that once made cars whose engines would not start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks like a factory; it is the flower. MORRIS was a British car make, gone now.
explanation.definitionFit: The orris is an iris whose root is dried for perfume, so it is a flowering garden species.

clue.text: Yeoman's complaint, chopping a tree

parts.note: a beef is a grievance or grumble

indicators.note: chopping breaks something up, so these letters are cut and reordered

explanation.surface: A farmer grumbles about felling a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chopping' rearranges A TREE into EATER. A Yeoman Warder guards the Tower of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Yeoman Warders of the Tower of London are popularly known by this nickname.
